title: Moroccan Director Yza Nouiga’s ‘Imichki’ to Make World Premiere at Toronto International Film Festival
content:
“Imichki,” a 15-minute short film directed by Moroccan-Canadian filmmaker Yza Nouiga, will make its world premiere in the fiction category at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), putting Morocco in the spotlight at this year’s festival.
Set in 1975 in a village in southern Morocco, the film follows Meriem, a young woman who has heard nothing from her husband after he left to work in France. Unable to read or write, she nevertheless does everything she can to send him a message, turning an impossible act into a quiet form of resistance against his absence and the limitations imposed by her world.
A Letter to Those Who Left
The film’s title comes from Tachelhit: imichki refers to those who left and never found their way back, people said to have forgotten their homeland. Nouiga said she explored the major waves of departures that shaped Morocco throughout the 20th century, from forced recruitment during the colonial period to rural exodus and the many people who sought to migrate to Europe or elsewhere in Africa. These departures left behind villages filled with stories of those who were absent.
While researching these stories, the director came across a traditional song, a timnadin, in which a woman expressed her wish to “be a letter, folded inside her beloved’s suitcase.” That image became the starting point for Nouiga’s screenplay. “That image opened up another world in my imagination. As I explored the stories of those who left, I came across the women who stayed behind. They spoke of absence with a restraint that moved me,” the director said.
Read also : Moroccan director Shaden Safieddine Tazi honored at Venice Film Festival
“Imichki” seeks to give shape to this sense of absence through Meriem’s eyes as she searches the landscape around her for a presence that has disappeared. “I felt that desire is strongest in what cannot be expressed. I imagined how this woman hoped to find the missing body again: through what path, through what gesture. By going to ask for news or by going to meet him. Perhaps it was through memories that she was best able to find him again. And as those memories were summoned again and again, they gradually turned into fantasies until they came to inhabit the landscape around her,” Nouiga continued.
About Yza Nouiga
Born and raised in Morocco, Yza Nouiga moved to Canada, where she studied screenwriting at INIS. She received the National Film Board of Canada award as part of the Talent Lab at the Montreal International Documentary Festival (RIDM) for her project “Jwad Amira.” Her previous short film, “Jardins Paradise,” had already screened at several festivals. Through her emerging body of work, the filmmaker repeatedly explores questions of heritage, transmission and women’s place in society.

title: California backs $18m tribal bid to buy 357 coastal acres for restoration
content:
California has approved $5 million towards the purchase of 357 coastal acres in Cayucos that once housed the largest abalone farm in the US. The yak titʸu titʸu yak tiłhini Northern Chumash Tribe is seeking to buy the property for $18 million and restore parts of the land and its former aquaculture operation.
According to The Tribune, the property, known as Alexander Ranch, has about one mile of coastline. It includes a eucalyptus grove that provides monarch butterfly habitat, a seasonal creek flowing into the Estero Bluffs and hills covered with grasses, sage and willow trees.
The tribe's nonprofit organisation entered into a purchase agreement with the estate of engineer John Alexander in 2024. The fundraising deadline is October 15, when the escrow period ends. As of June 2026, the organisation had raised almost $8.2 million, including a $7 million grant from California's Sustainable Agricultural Lands Conservation Program.
According to Becca Lucas Thomas, executive director of the ytt Northern Chumash Nonprofit, the land has a long connection with her people. Before Alexander used the property for aquaculture, it was home to an Indigenous village called tsitxala.
The tribe had harvested abalone from the coast for thousands of years.
“This property is really special. It holds a lot of history. To have the opportunity to bring this place back to our families today is really remarkable," Thomas says, as quoted by The Tribune.
Tribe plans restoration work
If the purchase goes through, the tribe plans to manage the property using indigenous stewardship practices. The proposed restoration work includes repairing habitats in the Villa Creek watershed, with the aim of supporting the return of steelhead trout.
The project is called yatspasini wa yaktspu Conservancy, meaning 'Ocean to land conservancy'. Lucas Thomas saysthe landscape had been actively managed by indigenous people before colonists forcibly removed them.
The tribe historically transplanted selected plant species, maintained waterways and used intentional burning to manage the landscape.
“While we look at this beautiful coastline, remember that it looks this way intentionally. It was created by our ancestors,” Thomas says.
The property also offers a place for the tribe to reconnect with its ancestral land. Thomas says members could eventually gather and camp there without having to seek permission from another landowner or rent a campsite.
The former abalone farm, closed in 2020, is part of the $18 million Alexander Ranch sought by the Northern Chumash Tribe.
Former abalone farm could reopen
The property also contains the remains of an abalone farm built during the 1960s. At its peak, the farm raised about 1 million abalone each year for meat.
The facility closed in 2020. About 900 concrete aquaculture tanks have remained unused since then. The Harmony Coast Aquaculture Institute currently leases the facility and wants to work with the tribe on bringing the farm back into operation.
Ben Ruttenberg, co-founder of the Harmony Coast Aquaculture Institute and director of Cal Poly's Center for Coastal Marine Sciences, said of ytt Tribe, "They are the perfect partner. This was originally their land.”
The institute also holds a state permit for the farm's seawater intake pipe. According to Ruttenberg, the pipe can bring in about 7,000 gallons of seawater per minute. He said such permits are very difficult to obtain and are important for an aquaculture operation.
The proposed system would use algae as part of the water treatment process. Seawater would first be pumped into an algae tank, where the algae would absorb nutrients. This would lower the water's carbon content and acidity before it reaches the abalone tanks.
That is important because abalone build their calcium carbonate shells more effectively in less acidic water. The farm could also use the algae as food for the abalone. The animals need large amounts of food and can take about five years to reach market size.
After passing through the abalone tanks, the water would have higher carbon content and acidity because of the animals' waste. It would therefore pass through another algae tank before being released back into the ocean.
“Our goal here is to produce excellent water that is better than the water we brought in, or at least cleaner and has less carbon dioxide than the water we pumped in,” Ruttenberg said.
Farm could support abalone restoration
The planned operation would not only focus on producing abalone for food. The tribe also hopes to use part of the facility for research and restoration.
The former farm raised red abalone. Lucas Thomas said the tribe hopes to continue raising red abalone while also working with endangered white and black abalone for restoration.
Black abalone are different from other abalone because they live in the intertidal zone. This is the part of the coast that is covered by the ocean during high tide and exposed to air during low tide. Other abalone species live in deeper water.
Tribal members recently surveying the property found black abalone along the coastline. Lucas Thomas said that could make the property a useful location for black abalone restoration work.
Scientists already understand how to raise white abalone in captivity and move them into the wild. However, there have been few successful attempts to raise black abalone on a farm.
Lucas Thomas said some of the existing aquaculture facility could be used to study how black abalone can be raised in captivity.
The project also has a cultural importance for the tribe because abalone has long been an important food source. California closed the recreational abalone fishery, while buying the molluscs has become expensive, leaving the tribe without consistent access to them.
“Many of our elders grew up with abalone being a fixture,” Lucas Thomas said. “That just hasn’t been a thing for 30, 40 years.”
Tribal members eat abalone and also use its shells to make jewellery and decorate regalia.
“To be able to have access not only back and steady, but within our control, as something that we’d be able to provide directly for our community. It’s a really, really important piece of this for us,” Lucas Thomas said.

title: El rugido del mar: bioacústica comunitaria para entender cómo el cambio climático afecta al pez mero del Caribe en México
content:
- En Punta Allen, Quintana Roo, miembros del Centro Comunitario de Investigación y Monitoreo Submarino (CECIMS) monitorean al mero del Caribe (Epinephelus striatus) con hidrófonos que escuchan su actividad durante la época de reproducción.
- Desde que la comunidad creó dos Zonas de Refugio Pesquero en 2016, las agregaciones reproductivas del mero han repuntado en un sitio casi extinto, registrando hasta 100 individuos por buceo y más de 1800 en el sitio de mayor presencia.
- La especie está en peligro crítico de extinción: desova cada año en los mismos sitios y bajo la misma luna, una constancia que facilita su sobrepesca: de los 28 sitios de agregación que recuerdan los pescadores, hoy solo seis están validados científicamente.
- Los sensores oceanográficos del CECIMS han documentado un aumento de al menos un grado en la temperatura del agua en una década, y durante el blanqueamiento masivo de corales de 2023-2024, el peor registrado a nivel mundial, captaron los picos de calentamiento en tiempo real.
Treinta metros bajo la superficie del mar, un sonido reverbera por el arrecife. Cientos de meros del Caribe (Epinephelus striatus) se congregan en un frenesí de cortejo que sucede una sola vez al año. Vocalizan. Cambian de color. Danzan en espiral unos alrededor de otros. El propósito: asegurar su reproducción. Su rugido particular se mezcla con otro sonido que resalta entre el bullicio. Con el regulador todavía puesto, Magdiel ‘Mako’ Naal, buzo y monitor comunitario, grita: «¡Ya se está recuperando San Juan!».
Este frenesí reproductivo y sonoro sucede en uno de los reservorios de biodiversidad más importantes de México: la Reserva de la Biosfera de Sian Ka’an, cuyo nombre significa ‘el origen del cielo’ en lengua maya. La reserva abarca más de 650 000 hectáreas de selva tropical, manglares y humedales que colindan con el Sistema Arrecifal Mesoamericano (SAM), la segunda barrera de coral más grande del mundo. El sitio es Patrimonio de la Humanidad declarado por la UNESCO desde 1987 y alberga una comunidad que existe mucho antes de su nombramiento. Punta Allen y sus 400 habitantes sostienen la historia de la cooperativa pesquera Vigía Chico.
En 2015, pescadoras y pescadores de la cooperativa se organizaron para crear el Centro Comunitario de Investigación y Monitoreo Submarino (CECIMS), el primero de su tipo en la región. Desde entonces, generan información científica que sustenta la renovación de dos Zonas de Refugio Pesquero en la Reserva, ubicada en el estado de Quintana Roo. Estos refugios son áreas protegidas federales que la propia comunidad propone, estudia y defiende. Para ello utilizan el monitoreo acústico pasivo: hidrófonos colocados en el fondo del arrecife que escuchan al mero durante su época de reproducción.
Entre 2017 y 2025 acumularon más de 8000 minutos de grabaciones submarinas y lograron registrar los diferentes sonidos de los peces, al punto de identificar con precisión las fechas de desove. Desde la implementación de los refugios, la cantidad de meros que llegan hasta la zona para reproducirse ha crecido, registrando hasta 3000 individuos por temporada en el sitio de mayor abundancia.
El mero del Caribe —también conocido como mero de Nassau o mero estriado— se encuentra en lo alto de la cadena alimenticia, justo por debajo de los tiburones. Es una especie importante para estos arrecifes, pero también una de las más vulnerables. Clasificado en Peligro Crítico de extinción por la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN), es solitario la mayor parte de su vida, pero entre enero y marzo abandona el aislamiento para congregarse de a miles en sitios específicos del arrecife y desovar bajo la luna llena. Siempre el mismo sitio y la misma luna. A estos eventos se les llama “agregaciones reproductivas”. Sin embargo, esa constancia que hace posible su reproducción también ha facilitado su sobrepesca y algunos de estos sitios ya han sido exterminados.
Científicos han identificado seis sitios de agregación en Quintana Roo, pero no fueron los primeros en hacerlo. Los pescadores más antiguos hablan de 28 sitios donde sucede —o sucedía— el espectáculo reproductivo. Uno de ellos es San Juan, que hoy es una de las dos Zonas de Refugio Pesquero que protege la cooperativa. Antes de que se prohibiera la extracción de especies durante los meses de las agregaciones reproductivas, cuentan en Punta Allen, los furtivos pescaban con dinamita y extrajeron toneladas de mero hasta acabar con ellos. En 2016, cuando la comunidad logró la creación del refugio, el sitio estaba dado por perdido. Una década de vigilancia y monitoreo más tarde, este año se volvieron a registrar más de cien meros del Caribe en la zona: una señal de que San Juan revive.
Pero lo que es una gran historia de éxito para los meros y los pobladores de Punta Allen está en peligro por una nueva amenaza: la crisis climática.
Los “meros-meros” del Caribe
«Es como un ronquido, como un rugido bastante grave. Rápidamente lo identificas porque no eres tú ni el compañero. Volteas y ahí está. Te está viendo y te está avisando que estás entrando en su zona». Así describe Magdiel Naal el encuentro con un mero del Caribe durante los buceos.
Naal es de los pocos nacidos en Punta Allen y actualmente sostiene la presidencia del CECIMS. El mar no es nada nuevo para él. «De pequeño me escapaba de la escuela y me escondía en la lancha de mi papá. Cuando se daban cuenta ya estábamos en altamar», recuerda. Su padre, Daniel, fue uno de los primeros buzos monitores de Punta Allen, de los que salieron a buscar las agregaciones de mero cuando nadie sabía bien qué eran ni para qué servían; mientras que su hijo, Jorge, comenzó a monitorear con solo 10 años y hoy, a los 22, es buzo de rescate y forma parte de la cuarta generación de monitores. «El mar te llama; quieres sentir la emoción de estar allá afuera», afirma Magdiel Naal.
A diferencia de las áreas marinas protegidas, que se establecen por decreto presidencial, las Zonas de Refugio Pesquero son una solución de las comunidades para las comunidades. Consideradas en la Ley General de Pesca y Acuacultura Sustentables, son propuestas por los propios pescadores y miembros de la comunidad, quienes definen qué especie proteger, en qué sitio y con qué objetivo. Pero no son un acuerdo opcional: sus reglas se publican en el Diario Oficial de la Federación y obligan a todos a seguirlas. Una vez aprobadas, tienen una duración de cinco años y deben renovarse con una justificación científica, explica Omar Rivera, mentor de cambio en Comunidad y Biodiversidad (COBI), una asociación civil que ha apoyado a cerca del 80 % de los refugios pesqueros mexicanos.
En Punta Allen hay dos zonas de refugio pesquero: Niche Habin y San Juan, que miden entre 15 y 17 km2 y van desde los 20 a los 100 metros de profundidad. Ambas se han renovado dos veces y buscan la protección de las agregaciones reproductivas del mero del Caribe. Para lograrlo, queda prohibido pescar mero durante la temporada de reproducción dentro de los polígonos marcados, y son los comités de vigilancia de la propia cooperativa quienes hacen cumplir la norma.
Pero el refugio pesquero es más que una figura legal. «Sirve como un faro», dice Rivera. «Ese faro trae una luz que ilumina muchas otras actividades». Desde su implementación, las zonas de refugio han fortalecido las capacidades técnicas y científicas de la comunidad, generado espacios de participación igualitaria dentro de la cooperativa, y transferido liderazgo a nuevas generaciones, sostiene el biólogo. En la práctica, cinco de los once miembros del CECIMS son mujeres y ya van cuatro generaciones de líderes comunitarios que se forman en buceo, monitoreo y conservación.
Distinguir el rugido del mero entre el ruido del arrecife en los miles de minutos de grabaciones exige una ayuda tecnológica que la comunidad por sí sola no puede construir. Por eso, el CECIMS y COBI se aliaron con el investigador Laurent M. Cherubin, de la Florida Atlantic University, para implementar un programa capaz de reconocer y aislar el sonido de las distintas especies de mero. Los hidrófonos se quedan uno o dos meses en el fondo del mar; después, las grabaciones son procesadas en Estados Unidos, el algoritmo separa las vocalizaciones del mero del resto del bullicio y los datos vuelven a Punta Allen convertidos en fechas y horas de actividad reproductiva clasificadas por especie. Es precisamente este resultado el que le permite a la cooperativa “espiar” a los meros durante las agregaciones reproductivas sin el costo ni el riesgo de bucear una y otra vez a 30 metros de profundidad.
Cuando las primeras grabaciones fueron analizadas por los investigadores en Florida, su programa identificó miles de meros tigre (Mycteroperca tigris) o alguna otra especie del género Mycteroperca. «Les dijimos: no es cierto, tu programa te está diciendo una mentira, no hemos visto más que dos o tres meros tigre en comparación con los miles de meros del Caribe que vemos durante las agregaciones», cuenta Rivera. En ese momento descubrieron que los meros del Caribe mexicano vocalizan diferente a los meros del Caribe estadounidense. Misma especie, distinto acento. Tan distinto que Rivera no descarta que futuros análisis genéticos revelen subespecies.
Esto llevó a que los investigadores recalibraran el algoritmo. Desde entonces, los datos regresan a Punta Allen procesados y precisos.
Esa precisión permite algo que antes era imposible: saber, sin bajar al agua, si la agregación reproductiva ya comenzó. «Ahí vemos la gráfica: en qué día, a qué hora, en qué fase de la luna», dice Magdiel Naal. Los hidrófonos también confirmaron algo que los pescadores más viejos ya intuían: al caer el sol, la actividad reproductiva se intensifica. «Se ponen más románticos en la tarde-noche», comenta Rivera.
Los informes se presentan cada año en asamblea ante toda la cooperativa y también se comparten con las autoridades gubernamentales que gestionan la reserva de Sian Ka’an. «Al principio no nos tomaban en cuenta», dice Naal sobre los directivos de la cooperativa. «Ya empezamos a mostrarles qué hacemos. Ahora ellos mismos preguntan: ‘¿cuántos viste?’ Nosotros se los presentamos: ‘esto es lo que vemos, esto es lo que escuchamos y esto es lo que pasa’. Con esa información [los directivos de la cooperativa] dicen: ‘okey, [están funcionando las zonas de refugio pesquero] vamos a renovar'».
¿Mal clima para los meros?
«Tu mente no entiende lo que tu vista ve», dice Lucía Cosgaya. Lleva dos temporadas buceando en las zonas de refugio pesquero de Punta Allen y recuerda así la primera vez que descendió a una agregación reproductiva de mero en Niche Habin. Contó 150 individuos en un cuadro mental y se rindió —eran miles—. Cosgaya no es bióloga ni pescadora, pero conoce los altibajos del mar mejor que muchos. Ella es cocinera tradicional, madre, vecina de la comunidad y esposa de un socio de la cooperativa que también es monitor del CECIMS.
Durante años vio salir a los buzos desde la orilla sin ser una de ellos, pues sus múltiples responsabilidades se entrelazaban con el prejuicio hacia la mujer en los entornos marinos. “De pequeña ni me dejaban esnorquelear”, cuenta. Hoy es monitora comunitaria del CECIMS y bucea a 30 metros de profundidad en condiciones que no son nada sencillas. “El miedo no se ha ido del todo. Cuando dicen ‘agregación’ empieza a retumbar mi corazón. Pero si logro entrar, todo cambia», dice Cosgaya. “Rompes tus barreras, rompes tus miedos. Te vuelves poderosa”.
Las agregaciones no ocurren en cualquier condición. «Solo están ahí cuando hay mal clima», sostiene Cosgaya. Y eso, «tiene una lógica aplastante» para la buceadora. El oleaje y las corrientes no son un obstáculo sino una necesidad biológica. Las larvas del mero logran dispersarse gracias a las fuertes corrientes que acompañan un “mal clima”. Estas condiciones les permiten alejarse de los depredadores y sobrevivir. Mientras que para los meros, el mal clima les permite subsistir, para los monitores, la travesía al sitio puede tomar más de una hora en esas condiciones difíciles. «La última vez que fuimos, un capitán quería regresar y el otro no», cuenta.
Sin embargo, lo que el cambio climático amenaza no es solo la temperatura del arrecife sino esta lógica de supervivencia: Si los patrones de corrientes se alteran, la dispersión de larvas se ve comprometida y con ella la variabilidad genética del mero del Caribe.
Un estudio de 2018 ya mostraba la fuerte relación entre calentamiento del océano, cambios en las corrientes marinas y en las agregaciones reproductivas del mero del Caribe. Ese calentamiento puede transformar las condiciones físicas que sostienen la reproducción del pez en el Gran Caribe y sus conexiones con el golfo de México. Al elevar la temperatura superficial del mar, el agua se vuelve menos densa y puede modificar la dinámica de las corrientes. Estos cambios son relevantes porque las agregaciones de desove de la especie se asocian con un intervalo térmico relativamente estrecho —entre 24 y 27.5 °C— y con determinadas condiciones de circulación. El estudio señala que el hábitat adecuado para las agregaciones reproductivas podría disminuir y desplazarse hacia el norte: una señal de alerta para una especie cuya reproducción depende de encuentros masivos, breves y sincronizados en sitios específicos.
Por eso, los sensores oceanográficos del CECIMS llevan una década registrando la temperatura del agua en los sitios de agregación y han documentado un cambio de al menos un grado en ese período. En los episodios más cálidos han llegado a marcar 31.5 grados centígrados a 30 metros de profundidad. Durante el blanqueamiento masivo de corales en 2023-2024 —el más grave hasta la fecha, pues afectó a más del 84 % de los arrecifes del mundo, incluido el SAM, según la NOAA— los sensores de Punta Allen captaron los picos de calentamiento en tiempo real. «Hemos visto cambios en los corales, como blanqueamiento y nuevas enfermedades», dice Lucía Cosgaya. Para ella, la consecuencia es obvia: “Dependemos de los corales. Si no hay corales vivos, no hay peces».
Leer más | Antártida: cierran la pesquería de kril por sobrepesca y crece la alerta por sus impactos
En las asambleas comunitarias, los datos dejan de ser sólo gráficas que reúnen temperatura, fecha, hora y actividad vocal del mero: se convierten en historias que tocan lo que sucede fuera del agua. «Para la gente no solo el agua estaba caliente», explica Rivera. El aire y el cuerpo también: «hubo menos pesca, más enfermedades y no sirvió la planta de luz en ciertos días». Los efectos del cambio climático y la sobrepesca no se los vienen a contar: los escuchan, los ven y los viven en su comunidad. Por lo mismo, «el conocimiento que a veces tanto nos gusta presumir, ellos lo tienen de una manera tan natural que no lo necesitan alardear», dice el biólogo. Este conocimiento anclado al territorio, sumado al dato preciso que la ciencia les ofrece, ha probado ser un gran aliado para la protección de su hogar.
Lo que a Rivera más le impacta es que, «a pesar de que son personas que llevan toda la vida viviendo allá, está esa capacidad de asombro, esa capacidad de orgullo de lo que representan esos sitios [de reproducción del mero del Caribe] para ellos». A Punta Allen la sostienen cuatro generaciones de pescadores que aprendieron a escuchar al mar incluso antes de que se interpretaran los datos. Ahora esos datos les devuelven lo que sus mayores intuían mirando la luna y las estrellas: el momento exacto en que el mero se reúne a cantar, danzar y desovar. «El mar representa todo para nosotros», dice Lucía Cosgaya. «El mar es vida», dice Magdiel Naal. «Un lugar estable, si lo cuidas», dice Jorge Naal. Daniel Naal no agrega nada más, solo escucha las olas.
Un Estado que no colabora
Durante todo el año el mero suele mostrar una coloración café-rojiza con barras claras. Pero en las agregaciones reproductivas su cuerpo cambia: aparecen fases adicionales —bicolor, oscura, de vientre claro—. En la zona, estudios recientes han documentado que esas fases son un lenguaje corporal con el que los peces coordinan el cortejo, la territorialidad, la disponibilidad reproductiva y, posiblemente, los roles dentro del desove. «Es como cuando ves a un ave hacer danzas aquí en la tierra, ahí abajo ves a los meros cortejando y danzando», describe Rivera. Al caer la tarde, el cortejo culmina: un grupo asciende de golpe y, al frente, una hembra libera los huevos mientras detrás los machos los fertilizan.
La norma mexicana que regula el aprovechamiento del mero abarca las costas del Golfo de México y el Caribe, pero fue diseñada en torno al mero rojo (Epinephelus morio), una especie que destaca en las pesquerías del Golfo pero que escasea en las del Caribe. De ahí vienen dos desajustes para el mero del Caribe. El primero, de talla: la norma fija una talla mínima de captura de 36.3 centímetros —por debajo de los 38 a 50 en que el mero del Caribe alcanza la madurez—, de modo que permite pescarlo antes de que llegue a reproducirse. El segundo, de calendario: la veda vigente para el Caribe mexicano va del 1° de febrero al 31 de marzo; y con el cambio climático, las fechas de desove cambian, señalan los investigadores. «La época de veda está desfasada», advierte Rivera. «Hemos visto que todavía hay meros en etapa de reproducción en meses en que la veda ya no está activa».
Para corregir los datos, COBI, junto con la Asociación Interamericana para la Defensa del Ambiente (AIDA) y el Fondo para el Sistema Arrecifal Mesoamericano (MAR Fund), recomiendan aumentar la talla mínima para incluir la talla de madurez del mero del Caribe, separar la veda del Golfo de la del Caribe y extender la de esta última región de dos a cuatro meses. También proponen reconocer oficialmente las agregaciones reproductivas como sitios de importancia crítica en la legislación pesquera mexicana, otro vacío que persiste. Un investigador de la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) trabaja actualmente en una propuesta para ajustar esa época de veda con base en los datos acústicos del CECIMS.
Los datos que recogen los pescadores mantienen de pie un refugio que le da a los meros la seguridad para multiplicarse. Con esa información, el CECIMS le comprueba a la cooperativa que los refugios funcionan y ésta destina más recursos para su renovación y vigilancia. Rivera explica que, según un informe reciente, se han logrado identificar y detener a más de cincuenta personas por pesca ilegal en la zona.
Y los meros notan la creciente protección: En Niche Habin las temporadas vuelven a reunir miles de meros; en San Juan, que pasó varios años sin ver un solo pez, ya empieza a repoblarse. «Todos estos factores sociales de gobernanza por parte de la comunidad, combinados con que existe un polígono de protección oficial, están haciendo su chamba [su trabajo]», dice Rivera.
Pero la Reserva de la Biosfera de Sian Ka’an y la comunidad costera de Punta Allen no están exentas de otras amenazas. Desde Tulum, uno de los polos de desarrollo más cercanos a la reserva, llegan la contaminación y los pescadores furtivos que activamente buscan los sitios con mayor biodiversidad. «Si se enteran de que hay un lugar bonito, ahí ya valió [ya no tiene futuro]», dice Jorge Naal, hijo de Magdiel y miembro de la cuarta generación de buzos monitores del CECIMS y quien ya cría a la quinta.
El proyecto Puerta al Mar —una carretera de 54 kilómetros que el Ejército mexicano construye a través de los humedales de Sian Ka’an hacia el Mar Caribe, y que incluye restaurantes, muelle y una playa artificial sobre manglares— preocupa a la comunidad por el modelo de desarrollo que podría atraer hacia las zonas de refugio. «Tiene implicaciones directas», advierte Rivera. «La intención de traer un modelo de desarrollo no compatible con lo que quieren las comunidades es una amenaza, sin duda». La cooperativa se ha opuesto formalmente al proyecto, asegura Magdiel Naal.
Daniel Naal tiene más de 40 años en Punta Allen. Ya no bucea, su columna se lo impide. Se le atribuye haber inventado la sombra para langostas, ese método ahora reconocido por su eficacia y utilizado en todo el Caribe para la pesca sostenible de estos crustáceos. Él fue uno de los primeros del pueblo en capacitarse como buzo y monitor comunitario, cuando nadie sabía a ciencia cierta qué era una agregación reproductiva ni para qué servía monitorearla. Hoy, su hijo Magdiel preside el CECIMS, su nieto Jorge ya participa en los monitoreos y acaba de convertirse en padre. «Ojalá crezca y conozca la especie», dice Daniel sobre su bisnieto. «Esto que hacemos es para las futuras generaciones, no para nosotros que ya vamos de salida».
*Imagen principal: Epinephelus striatus en su coloración café-rojiza. El mero del Caribe nace con gónadas sin una sexualidad definida. Hacia los cuatro o cinco años alcanza la madurez sexual y se establece como hembra o macho, un mecanismo poco estudiado. Foto: cortesía MarAlliance

title: Araceli y Mayte, trabajadoras sordas, ejemplo de inclusión laboral en centros especiales de empleo
content:
Araceli y Mayte, trabajadoras sordas, ejemplo de inclusión laboral en centros especiales de empleo
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
La tasa de empleo de las personas sordas se sitúa alrededor del 60%, superior a la media de las personas con discapacidad pero varios puntos por debajo de la población general.
A los 21 años, Araceli Pratdesaba empezó a notar que algo iba mal: le costaba distinguir sonidos superpuestos y seguir conversaciones en ambientes ruidosos. El diagnóstico llegó poco después: pérdida de audición en ambos oídos por una afectación del nervio auditivo. Con él, un largo proceso de aceptación que ella resume hoy con una frase: “Antes pensaba: ‘Y encima soy sorda’. Ahora digo: ‘Sí, soy sorda, ¿y qué?”.
La historia de Mayte Barroso no es muy diferente. Comenzó a notar una pérdida auditiva hace unos 20 años, cuando trabajaba en un puesto de oficina tras haber sido monitora de ocio y tiempo libre. Hoy, con una pérdida auditiva del 89% y de carácter degenerativo -cuyo posible origen genético todavía investigan los especialistas- Mayte usa audífonos en su día a día en su centro especial de empleo con total normalidad.
En el caso de Araceli, durante una década evitó los audífonos, hasta que el deseo de ganar independencia la llevó a dar el paso. Hace año y medio se incorporó como administrativa a una oficina en Barcelona de Integra CEE, uno de los centros especiales de empleo asociados a CONACEE, donde decidió apostar también por un segundo audífono para afrontar con seguridad sus nuevas funciones. Hoy trabaja con autonomía, se coordina con distintos equipos y describe el cambio como “un renacer”. En lo que respecta a Mayte, a su hipoacusia se suma una discapacidad visual que, no obstante, no le impide trabajar en Madrid como técnica de apoyo de otros empleados con discapacidad, incluidas otras personas sordas.
Una discapacidad que pasa desapercibida
Coincidiendo con la Semana Internacional de las Personas Sordas que se celebra hasta el próximo 27 de septiembre, la Confederación Nacional de Centros Especiales de Empleo (CONACEE) quiere poner nombre y rostro a una realidad que sus centros viven cada día: personas con discapacidad auditiva que, gracias a tener un empleo, han encontrado un espacio de autonomía e independencia. "Los ejemplos de Araceli y Mayte reflejan cómo los centros especiales de empleo (CEE) pueden transformar una discapacidad que a menudo pasa desapercibida en una fuente de desarrollo profesional", aseguran desde la entidad.
En este sentido, CONACEE recuerda que la tasa de empleo de las personas con discapacidad en España se sitúa en el 28,9%, frente al 69,7% de la población general, según datos del Instituto Nacional de Estadística. En el caso de las personas con discapacidad auditiva, la inserción laboral es mayor, pero sigue siendo muy baja, pues alrededor de la mitad de las personas sordas no trabajan, y su tasa de empleo es del 60%. Una brecha que, señala la patronal, se agrava en el caso de discapacidades como la auditiva, que al no percibirse a simple vista tienden a generar barreras de acceso al empleo que pasan desapercibidas tanto para las empresas como para la sociedad.
La inclusión no consiste solo en dar una oportunidad, sino en generar entornos de trabajo donde las capacidades de cada persona puedan desarrollarse
“Cuando hablamos de discapacidad, solemos pensar en lo que se ve. Pero hay discapacidades, como la hipoacusia, que no se perciben a simple vista y que, precisamente por eso, generan barreras de acceso al empleo que pasan desapercibidas. Los CEE llevamos años demostrando que, con los apoyos adecuados, estas barreras se pueden derribar”, afirma Albert Campabadal Blanco, presidente de CONACEE.
“Los casos de Araceli y Mayte muestran que la inclusión no consiste solo en dar una oportunidad, sino en generar entornos de trabajo donde las capacidades de cada persona puedan desarrollarse plenamente, con independencia de las barreras de partida. Eso es lo que hacemos en los CEE cada día”, concluye Campabadal.

Andhra’s traditional leather shadow-puppet theatre, where light and intricately crafted puppets bring stories from epics and folklore to life.
Traditional designs drawn at the entrances of Andhra homes as symbols of welcome and prosperity. At Bhogapuram, their geometric patterns appear as floor inlays across transition zones and gate entrances.

title: Building a Library in Wartime Paris
content:
The Germans began firing on Paris again on the fifth of August 1918. Mary Josephine Booth was familiar with the sound of the air raid sirens by then. If they came at night, she would jump out of her bed at the Hotel Petrograd, dress, take what valuables she had, and if the shelling was especially fierce, retreat to the basement. But if the sirens came during the day, then Booth, clad in her olive-green uniform, would remain at her post in an ornate building across the street from the Palais de L’Élysée. “We had to keep working to get the library ready to open,” she would later write.
Booth was one of hundreds of librarians who went to war alongside American troops during the First World War. In the summer of 1918, the 42-year-old woman from Illinois served with fellow recruits to the American Library Association’s Library War Service as they prepared to open an American library in the war-scarred French capital, pictures of which are now available from the American Library in Paris via JSTOR. Booth helped with unpacking and sorting the countless books that arrived from the home front, cataloguing titles for the new library (a project made more challenging by the lack of a Dewey Decimal reference guide) and selecting which would be sent to “our boys in the front trenches.”
When the United States entered the conflict, the American Library Association had not been well known. In fact, among other organizations doing war relief work, the ALA was, on occasion, mistaken for the American Laundry Association and the Australian Light Artillery. By 1920, the group would raise $5 million from the American public, build 36 camp library buildings, and distribute more than 10 million books and magazines to soldiers stationed at 5,000 locations across the United States and Europe.
Booth seemed like a natural fit for the Library War Service. She was a graduate of the Illinois State Library School, had worked as a librarian at Eastern Illinois Normal School for more than a dozen years, and she was eager to join the war effort in Europe. But the American Library Association did not initially warmly welcome women to the ranks of its war service. The organization saw the undertaking as an opportunity to masculinize the women-dominated profession, historian of librarianship Suzanne M. Stauffer says. Only men “of real executive ability” were officially permitted to be camp librarians, as the presence of women “would interfere with the freedom of the men in their camp life” and would deter “red-blooded he-readers” from using the libraries.
That was not Booth’s experience. She arrived in France in November 1917 as a Red Cross volunteer. Her first assignment was in a canteen at an aviation training center near Tours. There, she made ham, cheese, and jam sandwiches and built a makeshift library of her own. On January 21, 1918, she noted in her diary that there were “about 175 books ready to circulate,” purchased by a fellow canteener who had been given some money to “buy whatever was most needed.” Booth would later recall the popularity of the women’s library: “There were calls for mechanical books, as well as novels with lots of life and love, blood and thunder, and in contrast the poems of Milton and Browning.”
By 1918, the ALA had realized that it could not succeed in its mission without women librarians, though they were oftenrelegated to behind-the-scenes roles. In Europe, the director of the Army Library Service was Burton Stevenson, whose library at Camp Sherman in Ohio served as the basis for the Library War Service. Stevenson sometimes wondered how he, a Princeton dropout who became a librarian after marrying one, had achieved the position. He wrote to a friend from Paris, “my library work previous to about a year ago, was a sort of avocation, a sort of recreation which kept me in touch with books; so it seems strange to me sometimes that I should be the man selected to come to France to represent the A.L.A.” A photo in Stevenson’s office dated 1919 shows the American library staff. Booth, in her ALA uniform complete with tie, is gathered with five other women, including librarian-in-charge Elizabeth Gray Potter, and one other man.
The American library opened its doors at 10, Rue L’Élysée on August 29, 1918, as planned. The marble-columned entrance hall of the former home of the papal legate was taken up with a circulation desk; two large reception rooms with frescoed ceilings and mirrored walls had been converted into reading rooms; and the central hallway was lined with bookshelves for more than 7,000 titles. It was soon filled with men in khaki. “It was astonishing how quickly the soldiers discovered there was an American Library in Paris,” Potter noted.
Booth was quickly sent off on new missions. First, she organized the library of the new US military intelligence section (“several thousand books, English, French, Italian, German, especially strong in history, economics and military affairs”) and then, after the November 1918 armistice, she traveled through France sending books from the front back to Paris. “After the signing of the Armistice,” she later wrote, “the need of books was greater than ever; thousands of Americans in a strange land, all wanting to get home with nothing to do.”

"*" indicates required fields
Before returning to the library at Eastern Illinois Normal School (now Eastern Illinois University) in the summer of 1919, Booth’s last act was handing out magazines from the ALA to departing soldiers. She would go on to serve as a librarian at Eastern Illinois for another twenty-five years—and the American Library in Paris she helped to establish still exists today.

title: Coastal flooding occurs at predictable times, research reveals
content:
Coastal flooding may seem unpredictable, a natural disaster that occurs randomly. But UCF researcher Ivan Haigh has found that recurrent coastal floods occur at highly predictable times.
In a recent study published in Nature Communications, Haigh and a team of international researchers show that coastal flooding tends to occur at certain times of day, reflecting the timing of the tides. While previous research has largely focused on the seasonal timing of river and coastal flooding, this is the first study to show that floods with impacts have predictable daily timing across regions.
"Floods have traditionally been viewed as primarily weather-driven and therefore relatively unpredictable in their exact timing," Haigh says. "But surprisingly little attention has been paid to what hour of the day flooding occurs. Another reason is the way we measure flooding. We commonly talk about the number of 'flood days' per year. Once an event is reduced to a flood day, the information about whether the flooding happened at 3 a.m., 8 a.m. or 3 p.m. disappears."
Using tide gauge data and flood event records from the U.S. and the United Kingdom, the researchers found clear patterns in when floods occur. For example, in Boston, floods occur predominantly around noon and midnight, while in Southern California, they are more common in the morning. In Florida, the timing can vary along the coastline because the tides differ from location to location. Along the Atlantic Coast and down toward the Florida Keys, coastal flooding is moderately predictable, but along the Gulf Coast, flooding is less predictable.
Tides set the flood clock
Haigh says tides largely determine that predictability.
"In many locations, tides determine whether storm surge is sufficient to push water levels above flood thresholds," Haigh says. "As a result, even storm-driven flooding often inherits the timing of the tides."
The researchers also found that this phenomenon isn't unique to locations that experience semidiurnal tides, which consist of two high tides and two low tides each day. It also happens in places with diurnal tidal systems, with one high tide and one low tide per day, because of the way different tidal signals interact.
Rising seas heighten the stakes
As sea levels continue to rise, Haigh says coastal flooding is increasingly occurring without storms, making his findings more significant.
"This matters because timing influences impacts," Haigh says. "The same flood can have very different consequences if it occurs during the morning commute, business hours or in the middle of the night. Understanding these temporal patterns could improve flood forecasting, emergency planning, infrastructure operations and long-term coastal adaptation."
More precise warnings for coastal communities
Haigh says this work could improve existing flood forecasts, providing more warning before disasters occur. This can help people, businesses and emergency managers anticipate disruption and plan accordingly.
This information is also likely to become more useful as sea levels rise.
"Higher mean sea levels signify that it will take only a relatively small weather contribution or sometimes simply a very high astronomical tide to cross a flood threshold," Haigh says. "Understanding exactly when those critical tidal windows occur could therefore become an increasingly important component of coastal flood forecasting and preparedness."

title: Plant a Tree Day Origin and History: How Reforestation Grew to New Heights
content:
Our projects focus on restoring priority landscapes around the world—places where forests can make the biggest difference for nature and communities.
Click here to learn about our work
In the fall of 2018, 600 people showed up at 30 different sites — all to do the same thing: dig holes in the ground and put trees in them. By the end of the day, they'd planted more than 7,000 trees and shrubs. It was the very first Plant a Tree Day, and every year since, the event has grown into a global day for reforestation and celebration.
Plant a Tree Day is One Tree Planted’s annual day of action, held every Sept. 28, built to turn awareness of forest loss into planting, volunteering, and giving. It runs as a coordinated push across our network each year, timed to the start of fall planting season in the Northern Hemisphere, when the ground is ready for new roots. It's a day of action — getting new trees in the ground — and it’s also designed to prove that individual efforts can add up to something at landscape scale.
The day has since outgrown its founding numbers. We've now planted more than 171 million trees with 489 partners across 84 countries, and Plant a Tree Day has become the moment each year when we ask people to convert that broader mission into a personal action, whether that's organizing a local planting or giving directly toward reforestation efforts.
Planting in late September is also practical. Fall planting benefits from cooler air, steadier rainfall, and soil that's still warm enough for root growth to continue for weeks after leaves drop, giving new trees a head start before the stress of a hot, dry summer arrives.
We have seen firsthand that collective action scales in a way individual effort can't. A single donation or a single afternoon with a shovel may seem small on its own, but stacked against thousands of other people doing the same thing on the same day, it becomes visible, both to the volunteers themselves and to the partners and municipalities deciding whether reforestation is worth investing in.
The second reason for Plant a Tree Day is more sobering. The UN's Global Forest Goals Report 2026, drawn from voluntary national reports submitted by 48 countries representing 51 percent of the world's forest area, found that global forest area declined by more than 40 million hectares between 2015 and 2025.
The world has lost 420 million hectares of forest since 1990, an area larger than the entire European Union. The rate of loss has eased somewhat, from roughly 16 million hectares a year in the 1990s to about 10 million hectares annually between 2015 and 2020, but primary forest, the old-growth stands that took centuries to form and can't simply be replanted, has shrunk by more than 80 million hectares over the same three decades.
The UN’s own accounting shows progress, but not at the pace 2030 requires. Of the 26 targets tracked under the UN Strategic Plan for Forests, seven are broadly met and 17 are partially achieved, but two are off track entirely: reversing forest loss and eradicating extreme poverty among forest-dependent communities. "As 2030 approaches, the challenge is no longer only to recognize the value of forests but to scale implementation at the speed required," Juliette Biao, director of the United Nations Forum on Forests Secretariat at the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs said in a statement accompanying the report.
Ecosystem services from the world's forests, clean water filtration, flood control, pollination, and soil stabilization among them, are worth an estimated $16.2 trillion annually, with more than 1.6 billion people depending directly on forests for timber, food, fuel, and shelter, according to the UN.
Forests host 80% of the world's amphibian species, 75% of its bird species, and 68% of its mammal species, a concentration that makes forests the backbone of terrestrial life. Standing forests also currently absorb around 30% of the carbon dioxide humans emit each year, acting as one of the planet's largest active carbon sinks.
Shaded surfaces can run 20 to 45 degrees Fahrenheit cooler at peak temperatures than unshaded pavement or roofing, a gap wide enough to meaningfully lower cooling costs and heat-related illness in dense neighborhoods. A single tree can also draw between 10 and 150 gallons of water from the ground on a given day, releasing nearly all of it back into the atmosphere through transpiration and keeping less than 5% for its own growth, which is why tree cover often shows up in flood and drought management plans.
Community-organized events remain the backbone of Plant a Tree Day, and our forest fundraiser platform turns everyday personal milestones into reforestation campaigns, from a birthday, a marathon, or community challenge with the proceeds funneled straight into restoration work.
Donations made through Plant a Tree Day go toward restoring critical habitats and healing landscapes where the need is greatest, rather than being tied to a single, predetermined location. Membership in our Grove monthly giving community offers that same support on a recurring basis, at whatever amount someone chooses to set.
The UN is now pressing governments to support reforestation efforts. "Forests are essential to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, from climate action and biodiversity conservation to food security and resilient livelihoods," said Bjørg Sandkjær, Assistant Secretary-General for Policy Coordination at the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs. "Investing in forests is investing in climate stability, resilient economies and the well-being of present and future generations."
At its core, though, Plant a Tree Day is still individuals all around the world, in groups large or small, committed to putting roots in the ground because tree planting is an activity always worthy of an afternoon.
Jill Ettinger is a writer and editor covering the intersection of culture and sustainability. Her reporting connects our everyday choices to the environmental and social-justice stories shaping them, from the products we put in our carts to the communities a changing climate touches most. She is based in Los Angeles.

title: Welsh communities given support to build local energy projects to tackle climate change
content:
Welsh communities given support to build local energy projects to tackle climate change
Communities across Wales will receive a funding boost to build and control their own clean energy supply
- Great British Energy rolls out first wave of biggest public community energy investment in UK history, backing local places to cut bills and take climate action.
- Community energy groups can access more funding to build their own clean power projects.
- Communities to be offered an ownership stake in renewable energy projects, ensuring proceeds of clean power flow back into local areas.
Communities across Wales will receive a funding boost to build and control their own clean energy supply that will help to cut bills, grow local wealth and tackle the climate crisis – with the rollout of the biggest UK public investment in community energy.
Great British Energy is today (17 September) launching £30 million funding to kick start a community power revolution – the first downpayment on up to £1 billion, announced earlier this year - with the aim to support over 1000 local and community-led clean energy projects across the UK.
Building on Wales’ existing commitment to community energy through the Welsh Government Energy Service, the new funding will enable more community energy groups to accelerate plans for locally owned clean power projects - from solar panels on local buildings to village-owned wind farms and hydro schemes in nearby rivers. This will help to put money back in the pockets of communities and allow them join in UK-wide climate action, following the record temperatures reached this summer due to climate change.
These will be owned by community energy groups, meaning local areas can reap the full benefits – from reduced bills for local services to ensuring profits from the clean power generated flow back into towns and villages, rather than just to energy companies.
After the heatwaves and extreme weather events seen this year, this funding will expand communities’ opportunities to helping tackle climate change, building on the support provided by Welsh Government and its delivery partners - empowering them to move away from fossil fuels with their own clean energy supply that will help cut emissions and protect their local area.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said:
All of us felt deep concern for our climate during the record-breaking temperatures we experienced this summer.
Ahead of New York Climate week, we are putting power in the hands of people and places, so more communities can take action.
Everyone deserves a stake in our energy future and through these local power projects, communities can reap the full benefits of clean energy – reducing emissions, cutting bills and reinvesting profits to benefit local areas, instead of big energy companies.
Secretary of State for Wales Stephen Kinnock said:
Communities across Wales will be able to build more of their own clean energy projects with grants from the UK Government.
This project puts decision-making into the hands of local people, giving them the power to bring down household bills and be part of our national effort to tackle climate change.
CEO of Great British Energy Dan McGrail said:
Great British Energy is continuing to put communities at the heart of the clean energy transition with the GBE Community Fund and Partnerships Grant. Our vision is that every community should have the chance to build and own its own renewable energy. These grants will give community organisations and local authorities the practical support they need to get clean energy projects off the ground - lowering bills, supporting jobs and putting the benefits from energy into local hands.
Alongside funding specific local power projects, the government will also set out further details this Autumn on plans for community energy groups to be offered an ownership stake in renewable energy projects.
This aims to create partnerships between communities and developers that will see proceeds of clean power flow back into local areas. It will bring Britain in line with countries like Germany and Denmark, where this type of ownership set up is already widely used – allowing communities to benefit directly from local clean power.
Several such partnerships are already being developed in Wales and the work by GBE could help widen access to more communities.
Notes to Editors
-
Local ownership is already breathing new life into neighbourhoods across the country, reviving pubs, libraries and leisure centres. But for too long, community-run energy projects have been held back by a lack of funding, advice and government support.
-
Great British Energy is working with the Welsh Government to change this, as applications have opened today for new grants to support community energy projects Wales.in the first wave of up to £1 billion in support to put clean energy back in the hand of communities.
-
This builds on £9.5 million Great British Energy and the Welsh Government have already allocated to install solar panels on public buildings across Wales, such as schools, leisure centres and museums across, under the Welsh Government’s Wales Funding Programme. The funding has also backed the Welsh Government’s new Ymestyn scheme, which will help communities and the Welsh public sector to complete projects such as solar canopies and battery energy storage, to help cut energy bills and lower emissions. The Great British Energy support launched in Wales today includes:
-
The £20 million Community Fund - offers grant funding to help community organisations across England, Wales and Northern Ireland to test, develop and build community-owned clean energy assets. Projects supported by this fund must demonstrate that the community will hold a defined legal and financial interest in the project, and that a defined share of project benefits will be retained for, or delivered to, the local community.
-
Advice services – Great British Energy is also backing organisations that offer crucial advice to local groups on the development of community energy initiatives with £2.8 million support for advice services across England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
-
Great British Energy is also seeking information from investors to help size and scope its future products.

title: Itogon Mountain Village builds a home for love above the clouds
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Itogon Mountain Village in Benguet has transformed from a small family café into a popular mountain destination featuring cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel, all designed to showcase the stunning Cordillera landscape.
- The Bernabe family, who initially opened Café Stella, expanded their business in response to customer demand for private events, leading to the creation of additional facilities while preserving the natural environment.
- The venue emphasizes inclusivity and local culture, hosting various celebrations and working with local suppliers, while promoting environmental sustainability and heritage preservation in the rugged mountainous region.
ITOGON, Benguet – You notice the mountains before almost anything else.
They appear through the glass walls, between the pines beside the cabins, and behind the altar of a wooden chapel where nearly every direction opens to another ridge.
At Itogon Mountain Village, the view is not decoration. It is the point.
The three-hectare property in Barangay Loacan has grown from a small family café into a mountain destination with cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel designed around an almost 360-degree view of the Cordillera landscape.
On September 19, after weeks of habagat rain, the sun finally returned. The timing coincided with the property’s first wedding open house, Love Above the Clouds, but the experience made clear why people had begun coming here long before the flowers, gowns, and reception tables arrived.
The Bernabe family made a simple bet: that people would leave the city for the mountains, and that the mountains themselves were enough.
It started with coffee
Itogon Mountain Village did not begin with plans for weddings. It began with Café Stella.
“We started off very small,” said lawyer Rish Bernabe, one of the family members behind the property.
There were about six employees and only around 15 items on the menu, she recalled. Their father had envisioned a café down the mountain, while the family, which had long spent holidays in Baguio and the surrounding highlands, took on the challenge of running it.
Opening outside Baguio was a gamble. The place is almost half an hour away from the city, so “building up a business here was really a risk,” Rish said. Then people came.
The café gained attention on social media, and a kitchen designed for a modest number of customers suddenly had to feed far more. So they expanded the kitchen, upgraded to commercial equipment, hired more workers, and opened more of the building.
From a handful of employees, the enterprise eventually grew to around 80, according to the family.
Customers then began asking to reserve the café for private events. Closing the restaurant for an entire celebration was difficult, so the family expanded again.
Cabins followed. Then the Chapel of the Mountains. Then Montesierra, a dedicated events space.
What started as somewhere to eat had become somewhere people wanted to stay, gather, and mark important days.
Building around the mountain
The growth could easily have changed what drew people there. But the Bernabes say they tried not to let that happen.
Glass dominates much of the architecture so that the surrounding mountains remain visible. Buildings and roads were adjusted around existing trees whenever possible, they said.
One tree remains standing in the middle of a road because the family refused to cut it.
“This is the yamang lupa that made us come here,” Rish said. “So we really have to preserve it and celebrate it.”
That approach is most evident at the Chapel of the Mountains.
Wooden pews face an altar framed by glass, pines, and distant slopes. Light falls through the roof. Turn to either side, and the landscape remains part of the room.
On that sunny September afternoon, after a long stretch of rain, no manufactured backdrop could really compete.
The chapel is also deliberately non-sectarian. It is not accredited by the Roman Catholic Church to host Catholic sacramental weddings, management clarified after earlier confusion over a ceremony held there.
Rish said the couple involved had already been legally married in Manila and that the ceremony at the chapel was symbolic.
“We respect the rules of the diocese,” she said.
The space remains open to other ceremonies consistent with legal and religious requirements.
Its openness, then, is not only architectural. It gives couples and families from different traditions a place to celebrate in their own way.
Love beyond weddings
That idea of inclusion was central to the September 19 gathering.
“Today is about love, and not just romantic love,” said Suzy Mejia Bernabe, who handles marketing and sales for the family enterprise.
She spoke about weddings, birthdays, anniversaries, reunions, and other milestones, but also about creating a place where people could “slow down and reconnect.”
The family says it works with local suppliers, uses local produce when possible, and invites local makers, artists, and cultural performers to take part in events. That puts the property within a broader effort by Itogon to build tourism around its landscape and culture.
The municipality has long been associated with gold. Its own historical account traces gold working in the area to Indigenous communities before the colonial period, while large-scale mining later shaped much of the town’s modern history.
Today, Itogon’s tourism program also promotes nature and culture, with environmental sustainability, heritage preservation, and local employment among its stated goals.
The setting comes with limits. Itogon is rugged mountain country, with 74.6% of its land classified as having slopes steeper than 50%, according to the municipal government.
The Bernabes know building here is different from building on flatter ground. The terrain dictates what can be done, where structures can go, and sometimes which trees have to stay exactly where they are.
Perhaps that is why the place works. It does not feel as though the mountain was flattened to make room for a destination. In places, the destination appears to have negotiated with the mountain.
Looking up
For generations, Itogon has been known for what lies beneath its mountains: gold.
Itogon Mountain Village asks visitors to look up instead. At the pines growing beside the buildings. At the ridges beyond the glass. At a chapel where mountains remain visible behind the altar.
The family started with a small café and the uncertainty that anyone would drive this far from the city. But now, people come not only for coffee, but to stay, celebrate, marry, or simply spend a few hours where the mountains are allowed to remain the biggest thing in the room.
Perhaps the distance is not something visitors have to overcome after all. Perhaps it is part of the point. – Rappler.com

title: Two decades on, Nepal’s conservationists search for new ‘dream’ generation
content:
- In September 2006, a helicopter crash killed 24 people, including then forest minister and senior officials from Nepal’s government and WWF — a day after they handed over a conservation area to resident communities.
- Since the crash, some conservationists say individual roles were replaced, but what was lost was never truly recovered, with visionary leadership growing scarcer since the accident.
- Nepal’s tiger population has more than tripled and forest cover has grown beyond 46%, built on the community forestry model the “lost generation”, but human-wildlife conflict and the emptying of hill villages remain as unresolved conservation issues.
- Devolving control of buffer zones to local communities remains incomplete two decades on, and even the crash’s own commemoration has largely lapsed, leaving current leaders to decide whether to keep running the old conservation model or build a new one.
KATHMANDU — In September 2006, Nepal’s then Minister of Forests and Soil Conservation Gopal Rai and a contingent of conservation leaders flew to a remote village in eastern Nepal to hand over a conservation area to the people living there.
On the evening of Sept. 22, Rai handed over management of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area (KCA) to the community, hailing it as a milestone in Nepal’s conservation history. “For the community, this was the beginning,” Ghana Shyam Gurung, now WWF’s country representative, tells Mongabay.
The next day, minutes after take-off, the contingent’s Russian-built Mi-8 helicopter crashed, killing all 20 passengers and four crew. Among the dead were the forest minister, his spouse, senior officials, a Finnish diplomat, a senior USAID official and WWF staff. Bad weather hampered rescue efforts for two days. No one in the capital Kathmandu could confirm what had happened until searchers reached the wreckage.
Two decades later, the community-based approach to conservation pioneered by “dreamers” such as Harka and Chandra Gurung and Mingma Norbu Sherpa, all of whom were killed in the crash, still drives Nepal’s wildlife and forest recovery. The country’s tiger population has more than tripled and its forest cover has grown by six percentage points since the crash. But conservationists say progress has since stagnated.
A generation lost
The crash left empty seats at Nepal’s key conservation institutions. Conservationist Sarita Jnawali, then with the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC), remembers the day the deaths were confirmed. “When people like that weren’t there, we felt a huge sense of vacuum,” she tells Mongabay. “It felt like there was nothing left in conservation.”
At the forest ministry, then oint Secretary Krishna Chandra Paudel lost his minister and Acting Secretary Damodar Parajuli. At the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, ecologist Shiv Raj Bhatta lost his supervisors, director general Narayan Poudel and former director general Tirtha Man Maskey. The two were of such international stature, Bhatta says, that there was no one to replace them, “I wondered how we would ever produce people of that height again.”
WWF lost seven staff, “the single greatest loss of life in WWF’s 45-year history.” Among the dead was Mingma Norbu Sherpa, who had helped establish the Annapurna Conservation Area and led WWF Nepal at the time. “I’m a tough person,” Ghana Shyam Gurung from WWF says. “I could never endure that. That was hard..The hardest thing for me was meeting Mingma sir’s wife — meeting his widow. I haven’t cried that much even for my own mother. That was the first time.”
A wound that left scar
Paudel, who later served as the forest ministry’s secretary before retiring, describes the 20 years as a wound that left a deep scar. “It’s like when parents die suddenly, the family finds some comfort, and carries the ordinary rhythm of life forward,” he tells Mongabay. “But the old loss is never truly fulfilled.”
For Jnawali, the story of the past two decades is one of replacement, not continuity. “The vacuum I imagined didn’t happen, because people from a new generation took over,” she says. “They don’t remember the old story, but the vacuum still got replaced.”
Visionaries and people who dream a dream and see it through have grown scarcer, she says. This could be a result of government instability and weakening individual commitment as much as of the crash itself, she adds.
“In the absence of dreamers who could shift paradigms, what came after 2006 was largely the same work repeated,” she says, referring to the shift from strict, exclusionary conservation to community-based management pioneered and led by the people on the helicopter.
‘Have we stopped dreaming?’
Gurung says the difficult question to answer now is: Have we stopped dreaming after 2006? “We keep talking about the same things, redoing the same work,” he says. “So what’s next? Why aren’t we looking for new green areas?”
Conservation needs a breakthrough on the scale of the 1990s shift to community-based management, he says — one built around climate and water. He points to a model of coexistence suited to a landscape that now holds far more wildlife and far fewer farming families than it did in 2006. “The world ahead is about water,” he says.
Paudel disagrees with Gurung and Jnawali. Forest for Prosperity, the policy vision he says he pushed as secretary to tie conservation to household income, is a new dream by his own account. It aimed at prosperity rather than protection for its own sake. WIt was conservation becoming highly politicized that slowed the sector down, he argues, not that his generation stopped dreaming.
Missed opportunities
Jnawali counts the cost of the crash in missed opportunities for Nepal. Had the 2006 delegation lived, she says she believes that protected areas such as Annapurna and Manaslu might have followed Kanchenjunga into full community management, and new areas might have opened. “We didn’t just lose people that day,” she says. “We lost the pace we were moving at.”
Ecologist Bhatta traces the sector’s shortcomings to a failure of collaboration more than to the crash itself. Nepal’s community-based model won international recognition for biodiversity outcomes, he says. That model included the Terai Arc Landscape approach, a transboundary corridor of protected forests linking Nepal and India. But it delivered less on livelihoods, he says, because other ministries never fully joined in.
He says he wants devolution and to hand more control from the government to local communities. Buffer zones, areas around national parks, should be transferred more completely to community control, he says, with the park warden no longer the central authority. “The core was always local people,” he adds. That handover, in his view, is unfinished business.
Success in numbers
Nepal’s tiger population has grown from 121 in 2010 to a record 429 this year. Its rhino population has grown from 645 in 2015 to 752 in 2021. “We’ve increased tigers, we’ve increased rhinos,” former Secretary of the Ministry of Forests Paudel says. “That’s a result of the dream that generation was dreaming at the time.”
Part of that recovery rests on the community forestry system that the 2006 generation helped build. Nepal’s forest cover has grown from about 40% in the 1990s to more than 46% today — one of the sharpest reversals of deforestation anywhere. More than 23,000 community forest user groups now manage roughly 2.5 million hectares (6.2 million acres), and about a third of Nepal’s population belongs to one.
The cost of success
The recovering wildlife itself has become part of the strain. As tiger and rhino numbers have climbed, so has the toll of people killed or injured by the animals brought back by conservation efforts.
A 2026 study of Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape documented 245 tiger attacks on humans between 2010 and 2024 with 141 fatalities. The study also found a sharp surge in attacks in the Banke-Bardia complex between 2019 and 2023 — Bardia’s tiger population roughly doubled over the same period. Attacks declined after park authorities captured and relocated 21 tigers responsible for repeated conflicts, the study says.
Meanwhile, in the hills, people are abandoning their villages. In Taplejung, the district where the 2006 helicopter went down, data from officials in its Phungling Municipality reportedly say 245 to 330 families leave hill settlements every year with most citing crop losses due to monkeys.
A memory fading
In 2006 after the last rites of the deceased were performed and work resumed, the government instituted the National Conservation Day and a National Conservation Award to commemorate the memory of the deceased. WWF set up memorial scholarships that have since supported around 200 students, many of them women from underserved communities. More than 20 memorial scholars have gone on to pursue master’s degrees in New Zealand, according to WWF’s Gurung.
Two decades on, even the memory of the crash is fading unevenly. In Taplejung, a memorial features statue of the 24 deceased. In Kathmandu, the government-built statue park in Ramkot is overgrown and dilapidated, some names faded or gone. Paudel says observance of the disaster, once marked at the highest level of government, has all but lapsed. “Twenty years have passed and we have almost abandoned it for the last 10,” he says.
Local problems demand local solutions
Paudel says some progress has been made in tackling the challenges, but the measures don’t address the challenges completely. He points to compensation schemes for human-wildlife conflict deaths and insurance programs, both introduced since 2006, but argues that the answers Nepal needs next won’t come from Kathmandu. “Local governments should look for local solutions,” he says. “People know better.”
