title: After 11 hours, rescuers gave up on the boy in the well. Then a 14-year-old hero stepped in.
content:
In April 2013, a three-year-old boy named Gabriel fell into a well in the yard of his family’s home in Segarcea, a small town in Dolj County, Romania. The well was about 15 meters deep and barely wide enough for a slender teenager to squeeze through. Professional rescue crews arrived quickly. They tried everything available to them: shovels, a tractor, specialized equipment, different angles of approach. None of it worked. Hours passed.
After eleven hours, according to accounts that circulated widely at the time via CVL Press in Romania, a firefighter finally said aloud what everyone had started to fear: “There’s no more hope. The well is too narrow.”
At that moment, a 14-year-old boy named Cristian Marian Becheanu stepped forward. He was a seventh-grade student from the area, thin enough to fit where the adults could not. He told the crew he wasn’t afraid. He said he would go in.
Headfirst into the dark
They strapped a headlamp to his forehead, tied a rope to his ankles, and lowered him into the dark shaft headfirst.
Cristian went down with his arms stretched out in front of him so he could reach Gabriel once he found him. Somewhere in the dark, 15 meters below the surface, he did. When he emerged from the well with the three-year-old alive in his arms, the crowd that had gathered over those eleven hours erupted. Gabriel was taken immediately to hospital, where doctors monitored him for cervical spine injury and signs of oxygen deprivation. He recovered.
Reflecting on what he’d done, Cristian was characteristically understated. “I did what had to be done,” he wrote on Instagram. “I am proud of that act.” He also admitted, in accounts translated from the Romanian press, that he had been afraid at first. “But then I wasn’t,” he said.
Romania celebrated him. Local and regional officials honored Cristian at a ceremony at the Dolj County Prefecture. He received diplomas, a bicycle, a tablet, and a monthly stipend from the Artego Humanitarian Foundation through the end of 2013. Most significantly, county officials pledged support for the thing he said he actually wanted: to become a firefighter. As Alina Ionescu, director of the County Directorate for Sport and Youth, confirmed to CVL Press at the time, the institutions were committed to helping him pursue that path. Cristian is also the only civilian ever to receive the emblem of the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations, Romania’s highest emergency services honor, as reported by Romanian press in 2021.
He grew up to do it for real
He kept his promise. More than a decade after that night in Segarcea, Cristian Marian Becheanu is now Sergeant Major Cristian Marian Becheanu, a professional firefighter and rescuer with ISU Dolj, Dolj County’s official emergency inspectorate. He is married with children of his own.
The video of the rescue has resurfaced online repeatedly over the years, and its current wave of circulation is doing what it always does: stopping people mid-scroll. The details that get people every time are the ones the headlines often skip. That the well was 50 feet deep. That he went in headfirst. That a rope on his ankles was all that connected him to the surface. That two other volunteers stepped up before him, looked into that dark shaft, and decided they couldn’t do it.
Cristian decided he could.
This article originally appeared two years ago. It has been updated.

title: SBS aprueba reglamento para gestionar riesgo de sobreendeudamiento cooperativo
content:
La Superintendencia de Banca, Seguros y AFP (SBS) aprobó el Reglamento para la administración del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento de los socios deudores minoristas de las cooperativas de ahorro y crédito no autorizadas a captar recursos del público (Coopac), con el objetivo de fortalecer la gestión de dicho riesgo en el sistema cooperativo.


El reglamento busca promover el crecimiento responsable y sostenible de las colocaciones, sobre la base de una adecuada evaluación de su capacidad de pago.
En ese sentido, la norma establece estándares mínimos para la administración del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento. De igual modo, se incorporan reportes diseñados como herramientas de gestión —tableros de control— para que los funcionarios y directivos de las Coopac evalúen, monitoreen y realicen el seguimiento de dicho riesgo.
Para una adecuada gestión del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento, la norma también precisa responsabilidades para el Consejo de Administración y la Gerencia General, así como funciones específicas para el Comité de Riesgos, la Unidad de Riesgos y la Unidad de Auditoría Interna.
Cabe destacar que, la SBS – en el marco de su compromiso con el fortalecimiento del sistema cooperativo – lleva varios meses desarrollando talleres teóricos y prácticos, dirigidos a los funcionarios y directivos de las Coopac, sobre la gestión del riesgo de sobreendeudamiento y la elaboración e implementación de los reportes previstos en el reglamento; los cuales se tiene previsto continuar desarrollando en las próximas semanas a fin de fortalecer su desarrollo y adecuada implementación.

title: Phillip Island removed foxes; little penguin colony grew from 12,000 to 40,000
content:
Phillip Island’s little penguins once faced a crisis that threatened to erase much of their presence from the island. By the 1980s, nine of its 10 penguin colonies had disappeared, while the final colony on the Summerland Peninsula was also under pressure from introduced predators, habitat loss and human activity. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, a long-running conservation effort combining fox control, habitat restoration, scientific research and land rehabilitation helped reverse that decline. The surviving little-penguin population grew from about 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today. The story, detailed in the organisation’s pest-control, research and history records, shows how protecting wildlife often requires more than removing a single threat—it demands sustained cooperation between scientists, governments, local communities and visitors. Read on to know more:
A predator that changed the island
Phillip Island, also known as Milawul, is famous for the nightly arrival of little penguins at the Penguin Parade. Yet the sight that attracts visitors today was once at risk of disappearing.
Red foxes were introduced to Phillip Island in the early 1900s. Over time, they became one of the most serious threats to the island’s wildlife. Little penguins are especially vulnerable because they spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, moult and raise their chicks. Their nests are often located in burrows or sheltered areas close to the coast, where they can be exposed to predators.
Phillip Island Nature Parks describes foxes as the little penguins’ biggest threat on land. By the 1980s, nine of the island’s 10 penguin colonies had become extinct. The remaining colony on the Summerland Peninsula, which includes the Penguin Parade, was also under threat.
The decline was not caused by foxes alone. Research identified several other pressures, including habitat destruction, housing development, traffic near penguin colonies, fire and domestic pets. Together, these threats made it increasingly difficult for penguins to survive and breed successfully.
Warning signs from research
The island’s conservation response was shaped by research. Population studies conducted during the 1980s showed that the last remaining penguin colony could disappear by the late 1990s if existing threats continued.
That warning encouraged authorities and conservation groups to take action. The Penguin Protection Plan, announced in 1985, included scientific research, habitat management, a fox-control program and the gradual buyback of houses in the Summerland Estate.
The housing estate had been built within the penguins’ habitat. As houses, roads and associated infrastructure were removed, the land could be returned to a more natural condition. This was a major undertaking and required years of planning, funding and rehabilitation.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says the buyback and removal of the Summerland Estate continued for decades, as per reports. The final houses and infrastructure were removed in 2010, after which an ongoing rehabilitation program was established to help penguins and other wildlife thrive.
This approach recognised an important conservation principle: removing a predator is not enough if the habitat remains unsafe. Wildlife needs places to shelter, feed, breed and raise young without constant disturbance.
The campaign against foxes
Fox control began as a coordinated effort involving farmers, rangers and conservation workers. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, more than 1,000 foxes were removed over a period of 20 years.
The organisation initiated a dedicated Fox Eradication Project in 2006. Rather than relying on one method, the project used an integrated approach involving different techniques to locate and remove foxes across the island.
The goal was ambitious. Instead of simply reducing fox numbers, conservation teams aimed to remove foxes from Phillip Island altogether. This was important because even a small number of predators could threaten vulnerable colonies and prevent other species from recovering.
The campaign required persistent monitoring. Rangers and other workers had to search for signs of foxes, respond to sightings and prevent the animals from re-establishing a population. The work also formed part of wider pest management on the island, including programs targeting feral and roaming cats and rabbits.
In 2017, Phillip Island was declared fox-free after an intensive 20-year eradication program. The campaign was supported by the Victorian Government, Penguin Parade visitors, the Penguin Foundation and the Helen Macpherson Smith Trust.
Habitat restoration made a difference
The recovery of the little penguins was closely connected to the restoration of their habitat.
The Summerland Peninsula had once been transformed by housing development and human activity. Removing the houses allowed conservation teams to rebuild a landscape better suited to wildlife. The rehabilitation work helped restore vegetation, reduce disturbance and create safer areas for nesting.
The return of natural habitat also benefited species beyond little penguins. Short-tailed shearwaters and other coastal birds use the island’s protected areas, while the fox-free environment later supported the reintroduction of eastern barred bandicoots.
In 2017, the same year Phillip Island was declared fox-free, researchers released eastern barred bandicoots onto the Summerland Peninsula. The area had been rehabilitated from a former housing estate into a natural environment that supported a thriving little-penguin colony and migratory short-tailed shearwaters.
This illustrates how conservation gains can extend across an ecosystem. Protecting one habitat can create opportunities for several threatened species, especially when predators are controlled and human disturbance is reduced.
From 12,000 to 40,000 penguins
Phillip Island Nature Parks reports that extensive conservation work helped increase the number of little penguins from approximately 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today.
The figures represent more than a simple population increase. They reflect the combined effect of predator control, habitat restoration, reduced development pressure, scientific monitoring and community involvement.
The Penguin Parade also provides a useful way to monitor changes. Guides count the number of penguins crossing the beach each night, and annual averages can offer insight into population trends. These counts do not represent every penguin on the island, but they help researchers track changes in the colony over time.
Conservation teams also monitor breeding success by studying the number of chicks fledged per breeding pair at selected sites. This helps researchers understand not only how many penguins return to land, but also whether they are successfully reproducing.
Such long-term monitoring is essential because wildlife populations can change in response to food availability, disease, weather, marine conditions, human activity and other factors. Regular data collection allows managers to identify problems early and adjust conservation strategies.
Research continues on land and sea
Although the fox eradication campaign was a major achievement, the work of protecting little penguins has not ended.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says its researchers study penguins in both terrestrial and marine environments. This is necessary because little penguins spend around 80 per cent of their time at sea, even though they depend on land for breeding.
Researchers use GPS trackers and other devices to study where penguins travel for food. Tracking has shown that many penguins feed within 50 kilometres of the island’s colony, while some individuals travel farther during winter, including towards Portland in Victoria and Port Phillip Bay near Melbourne.
Understanding these movements helps scientists identify potential threats in the marine environment. Changes in ocean temperature, prey availability, pollution and human activity can all affect the penguins’ ability to find food.
Research projects also examine feeding hotspots by combining information about where penguins go, how much they eat and what prey they consume. This evidence can help guide future conservation decisions as marine ecosystems respond to environmental change.
A model for community-led conservation
Phillip Island’s recovery story shows that successful conservation rarely happens through one dramatic action. It is usually built through many years of practical work.
The fox eradication program required rangers, farmers, scientists, government agencies, conservation organisations and local residents to work towards the same goal. Visitors also contributed through tourism, with Phillip Island Nature Parks stating that visits help fund research and wildlife conservation.
The island’s history also highlights the importance of acknowledging the Bunurong people, the Traditional Owners of Milawul. Phillip Island Nature Parks recognises the continuing connection of the Bunurong to the landscape and describes its role in healing Country and supporting Traditional Owner involvement in decisions about Country.
The little penguins’ recovery is therefore not only a story about numbers. It is a story about restoring a damaged landscape, learning from scientific evidence and changing the way people share space with wildlife.
What the future depends on
The increase from 12,000 to 40,000 little penguins is encouraging, but it does not mean the species is permanently secure on Phillip Island. Conservation gains must be maintained.
Foxes must remain absent. Other introduced predators, including feral and roaming cats, require continued management. Roads, pets, fires, rubbish, human disturbance and habitat damage can still affect wildlife.
The penguins’ time at sea also creates challenges that cannot be solved entirely on land. Their food supply may be influenced by changing ocean conditions, climate change and human activity. That is why Phillip Island’s conservation program combines population counts, breeding studies, tracking and marine research.
The lesson from Phillip Island is clear: wildlife recovery becomes possible when threats are identified early and addressed consistently. A colony that once appeared destined to vanish has grown substantially because people chose to protect its habitat, remove its predators and continue monitoring its future.
For the little penguins returning to shore each evening, that long-term commitment has made the difference between disappearance and survival.

RESEARCHERS FROM UNIVERSITY of Galway are part of an international team working to restore deep-sea coral reefs damaged by bottom trawling by installing 3D-printed artificial reefs.
The research has seen 23 artificial reefs placed on the deep seabed off the south-west Porcupine Bank, off the west coast of Ireland and in the Bay of Biscay, France.
The early results are said to be “very encouraging” and researchers said the work could “open up new possibilities to scale up the restoration of damaged coral reefs elsewhere in the Atlantic and beyond”.
It’s part of a Horizon Europe project titled ‘REDRESS’, which is an acronym for “Restoration of deep-sea habitats to rebuild European Seas”.
The expedition to deploy the artificial reefs took place last month on board L’Atalante, a vessel of the French Oceanographic Fleet.
Reefs were placed at depths between 900 and 1,100m off the Porcupine Bank, and in the Guilvinec Canyon, Bay of Biscay – other reefs were installed here during an expedition last year too.
While cold-water coral reefs are less well-known than their tropical cousins, they provide important habitats for marine life and support biodiversity in the deep-sea, including fish.
The corals, however, are quite fragile and easily damaged by deep-sea trawling.
While recent fisheries and conservation regulations prohibit trawling in many areas where corals are found, the issue is now turning to how to return damaged areas to full health.
The artificial reefs are eco-designed cylinders made from low-carbon concrete incorporating volcanic material.
Each 3D-printed structure is around 80cm high and 100cm in diameter, weighing around 600kg.
They provide complex physical microhabitats including tunnels, ledges and overhangs, that offer shelter and provide surfaces for corals and other marine life to colonise.
The reefs are placed individually on the seabed, rather than together, to form a single connected structure covering an area of about half a hectare.
Researchers will monitor the sites over the coming years through photography, video and 3D mapping to assess how the coral and other marine life develop on and around the reefs.
Different approaches are also being tested as part of the research.
Some reefs were equipped with oyster shells, ceramic plates and tiles to encourage coral larvae to settle naturally, while others were fitted with fragments of living coral.
The aim is to see whether the coral can survive and establish new colonies or enhance the attractiveness of the artificial reefs for colonisation by coral larvae.
Encouragingly, researchers have found that the coral fragments, known as nubbins, which were placed on artificial reefs last year are still alive.
The reefs have also been colonised by a range of marine species, including sea urchins, fish, crabs and crinoids.
The research will also monitor seawater conditions, sediment and chemical contaminants.
This will help improve understanding of the conditions needed for healthy coral growth and assess the potential impact of climate change and ocean acidification on restoration efforts.
Both restoration sites, meanwhile, are now protected from further damage by bottom trawling.
Dr Anthony Grehan, a deep-sea ecologist at University of Galway and co-leader of the mission to the Porcupine Bank, said these “deep-sea coral reefs provide vital habitat for a diversity of marine life, but many have been damaged over many years”.
“Because these corals grow by only a few millimetres each year, natural recovery of lost reefs can take decades to centuries.
“With this project, we are testing whether we can actively accelerate that recovery by creating new starter structures for corals to grow on, which also mimic reef structure to help re-establish functioning reef habitats.”
Grehan said the “early results are very encouraging” and added: “If we can show that these approaches work, it could open up new possibilities to scale up the restoration of damaged coral reefs elsewhere in the Atlantic and beyond.”
Meanwhile, Marie-Claire Fabri, a research engineer in deep-sea benthic ecology and co-leader of the Bay of Biscay region expedition, remarked that “preserving these areas alone is not enough” and called for the “active restoration of cold-water corals”.
“The ban on bottom trawling has helped stop the direct pressure on these habitats, but to go further – given the slow growth of these corals in the Atlantic – just a few millimetres per year—we cannot simply wait for them to recover on their own.”

title: Gaza children return to in-person schools for first time in 3 years
content:
Gaza children return to in-person schools for first time in 3 years
The move is a fragile milestone; the conflict with Israel has killed around 22,000 youngsters and over 770 education workers
Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza have returned to in-person teaching for the first time in nearly three years, albeit in damaged or makeshift school buildings and tents, and with uniforms, notebooks and pens unaffordable for many families.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (Unicef) says 98 per cent of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war, and Gaza education officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education.
The reopening on Saturday was a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis.
“The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness and success,” said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis.
